metadata.title: PIRLS 2006 Technical Report
metadata.venue: TIMSS & PIRLS International Study Center, Lynch School of Education, Boston College

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: PIRLS 2006 used a two-stage stratified cluster probability design: schools were sampled first, and intact classrooms from the target fourth grade were sampled second. The report describes procedures for calculating sampling weights and participation rates (Chapter 9), and it also emphasizes minimum participation thresholds (e.g., about 85% for both schools and students, or a combined product rate of 75%). Because this is a technical report describing the assessment design, scaling, and database creation rather than an empirical ML analysis, the manuscript does not specify a particular weight variable name (e.g., W_FSTUWT) for a fitted model. For analyses using the PIRLS international database, analysts should apply the PIRLS sampling weights and account for the complex survey design when estimating population-representative statistics and standard errors.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This technical report describes PIRLS scaling using plausible-value technology, but it does not document a specific missing-data handling strategy for an empirical model (e.g., listwise deletion vs. imputation) because the document is focused on assessment construction and reporting procedures rather than a single fitted predictive model. Missingness in PIRLS is typically addressed through the PV framework and the international database preparation process, but the exact analytic rule is not specified in the provided text. Therefore, missing-data handling is treated as not reported for this extraction.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The report targets students enrolled in the fourth grade of formal schooling (with an age policy that the average age in the tested grade should not be below 9.5 years). The analytic population is drawn from probability samples using a two-stage stratified cluster design: sampled schools and then intact classrooms within the target grade. The report also notes participation requirements (minimum acceptable participation rates for schools and students) and that translation/language administration varies by country, but it does not specify additional analytic exclusions for a particular empirical model in the provided text.

data.outcome_summary: PIRLS 2006 is an international reading assessment administered to fourth-grade students (typically age-appropriate for reading-to-learn) using a rotated booklet design. The reading test comprises 10 passages (5 literary, 5 informational) with about 12 questions per passage and 126 total items, with a subset of passages retained from PIRLS 2001 to support trend measurement. Students are tested for 80 minutes (two passages) and complete a Student Questionnaire with additional time. The report describes a two-stage stratified cluster sampling design (schools, then intact classrooms) and emphasizes participation thresholds for data quality. Achievement is scaled using IRT models and reported using plausible-value technology, with international benchmarks derived via scale anchoring. The document is a technical guide to instrument development, translation verification, database creation, scaling, and reporting procedures rather than an empirical predictive study.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This document is a PIRLS 2006 technical report describing assessment framework, sampling design, translation procedures, database creation, and IRT scaling with plausible values. It does not present an empirical machine-learning model with a student-level target variable, performance metrics, or a fitted predictive pipeline; therefore, fields such as total_students, ML techniques, and main findings are not applicable for this extraction.
